body.text: On a kitenge cloth the same shape appears again and again, flipped, turned or made bigger. Computers draw such patterns using matrices. Earlier you reflected, rotated and enlarged shapes by drawing. Now you will do it with 2 × 2 matrices.
How a matrix moves a point

A transformation moves or changes a shape on a grid. Many transformations that keep the origin fixed can be written as a 2 × 2 matrix. To find the image of a point (x, y), write the point as a column vector. Then multiply it by the matrix, with the matrix on the left.

body.latex: \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} ax + by \\ cx + dy \end{pmatrix}
body.speech: the matrix a, b, c, d times the column x, y equals the column a x plus b y, c x plus d y

body.text: The quickest way to find a matrix uses the unit points I(1, 0) and J(0, 1). The image of I becomes the first column of the matrix. The image of J becomes the second column.
Matrices for reflection, rotation and enlargement
Each matrix below is written by its rows. Check each one by finding where it sends I and J.

items: Reflection in the x-axis: rows 1, 0 and 0, −1.
Reflection in the y-axis: rows −1, 0 and 0, 1.
Reflection in the line y = x: rows 0, 1 and 1, 0.
Reflection in the line y = −x, also written x + y = 0: rows 0, −1 and −1, 0.
Rotation of 90° anticlockwise about the origin: I goes to (0, 1) and J goes to (−1, 0). Rows 0, −1 and 1, 0.
Rotation of 180° about the origin: rows −1, 0 and 0, −1.
Rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin: rows 0, 1 and −1, 0.
Enlargement with centre the origin and scale factor k: rows k, 0 and 0, k.

body.text: For a rotation anticlockwise through any angle θ about the origin, the matrix is:

body.speech: the matrix with rows cos theta, minus sin theta and sin theta, cos theta

body.text: Finding the image of a shape

body.title: Rotate a triangle through 90° anticlockwise
steps: Triangle T1 has corners (1, 1), (5, 1) and (5, 3).
Write the corners as the columns of a 2 × 3 matrix: rows 1, 5, 5 and 1, 1, 3.
The rotation matrix has rows 0, −1 and 1, 0.
Top row of the answer: 0 × x + (−1) × y = −y, giving −1, −1, −3.
Bottom row of the answer: 1 × x + 0 × y = x, giving 1, 5, 5.
The image has corners (−1, 1), (−1, 5) and (−3, 5).

body.text: Finding the matrix from an object and its image

body.title: Find the matrix that maps a square
steps: Square OABC has O(0, 0), A(3, 0), B(3, 3) and C(0, 3). Its image has O fixed, A′(4, 2), B′(6, 6) and C′(2, 4).
Let the matrix have rows a, b and c, d. It sends A(3, 0) to (3a, 3c) = (4, 2), so a = 4/3 and c = 2/3.
It sends C(0, 3) to (3b, 3d) = (2, 4), so b = 2/3 and d = 4/3.
The matrix is one third of the matrix with rows 4, 2 and 2, 4.

body.text: The determinant tells you how the area changes. The area scale factor is the size of the determinant, ignoring any minus sign. A negative determinant means the shape has been flipped over, as in a reflection. A determinant of 0 squashes the shape onto a line.

body.speech: area of image equals the size of the determinant of M, times area of object

body.text: In the square example, det M = (4/3)(4/3) − (2/3)(2/3) = 16/9 − 4/9 = 4/3. The square has area 3 × 3 = 9 square units. So the image has area 9 × 4/3 = 12 square units.
The inverse matrix undoes a transformation
If M maps an object onto its image, the inverse matrix M⁻¹ maps the image back onto the object. Find it with the inverse formula from the Matrices topic.

body.title: Find the object from its image
steps: The matrix M has rows 2, 1 and 1, 1. A point P is mapped onto P′(7, 4). Find P.
M⁻¹ has rows 1, −1 and −1, 2.

body.text: Carrying out one transformation and then another is called a successive transformation. If A is done first and then B, the single matrix is BA. The matrix next to the point acts first, so read the product from right to left. In general AB and BA are different, so the order matters.

body.title: Reflect, then rotate
steps: A is reflection in the x-axis, with rows 1, 0 and 0, −1. B is rotation of 90° anticlockwise, with rows 0, −1 and 1, 0.
A first, then B: BA has rows 0, 1 and 1, 0. This is reflection in the line y = x.
B first, then A: AB has rows 0, −1 and −1, 0. This is reflection in the line y = −x.
The two orders give different single transformations.

body.title: Matrices from triangles
body.text: On grid paper, plot triangles T1 (1, 1), (5, 1), (5, 3); T3 (−1, 1), (−5, 1), (−5, 3); and T4 (−1, −1), (−5, −1), (−5, −3). In pairs, describe a single transformation that maps T3 onto T1, and one that maps T4 onto T3. Find where each sends I(1, 0) and J(0, 1), write its matrix, then find the matrix that undoes it.
A reflection matrix has determinant −1 and a rotation matrix has determinant +1. Both keep the area the same. What does the sign of the determinant tell you about the shape?

The images of I(1, 0) and J(0, 1) give the two columns of a transformation matrix. Multiply the matrix by a point to find its image, and use the inverse matrix to find the object. The size of the determinant is the area scale factor. For A followed by B, use the single matrix BA.
